description: Bear-baiting, cock-fighting and the playhouse — Elizabethan entertainment and who disapproved.
content_html:
Entertainment in Elizabethan England

Entertainment in Elizabethan England reflected the sharp divisions of society. The wealthy enjoyed elaborate banquets, hunting, jousting and masques at court, while ordinary people found pleasure in sports, festivals, taverns and, increasingly, the professional theatre. Both groups shared a taste for some forms of entertainment that modern audiences find uncomfortable — particularly the cruel animal sports that drew large crowds across the country.

Cruel Sports: Bear-Baiting and Cock-Fighting

Bear-baiting was one of the most popular entertainments of the age, enjoyed by people of all social classes — including Elizabeth I herself. A bear would be chained to a post in a circular arena (a “bear garden”) and set upon by trained dogs. London had several bear gardens on the south bank of the Thames, near what would become the theatre district. Cock-fighting was equally widespread, with purpose-built cockpits in many towns. Both sports involved gambling, which added to their appeal for spectators at all social levels.

These entertainments were not considered cruel in the way we would regard them today. They were a normal part of Elizabethan life, enjoyed on public holidays and Sundays. Puritans objected, but largely on moral grounds: they worried that such entertainments drew people away from church attendance and encouraged idleness and gambling, rather than expressing concern for the animals.

Key Fact

Bear-baiting was enjoyed by all social classes, including Elizabeth I. Puritans opposed it not for reasons of animal welfare but because it encouraged idleness and gambling, and drew people away from church on Sundays.

Entertainment for the Wealthy

The Elizabethan nobility and upper gentry enjoyed a range of pastimes unavailable to ordinary people. Hunting and hawking required land, horses and trained birds — luxuries of the rich. The royal court was a centre of culture: music, dancing and poetry were all prized accomplishments. Elizabeth I herself was an accomplished musician and dancer. Court masques were lavish productions combining music, dance, poetry and magnificent costumes. Tournaments and jousting continued into the early years of Elizabeth’s reign, though they declined in popularity as the century progressed. For those below the highest nobility, bowling, tennis and archery were popular, with archery practice actually required by law for men of certain ages.

The Rise of the Elizabethan Theatre

The most significant cultural development of the Elizabethan age was the rise of the professional playhouse. Before this period, plays were performed by travelling companies in inn yards, market squares or at court. The first permanent public playhouse in England, known simply as “The Theatre,” was built in Shoreditch, London, in 1576 by James Burbage. This was a pivotal moment: it created a permanent commercial theatre industry. More playhouses followed — the Curtain (1577), the Rose (1587), the Swan (c.1595) and, most famously, the Globe Theatre, built in Southwark in 1599 by the company known as the Lord Chamberlain’s Men.

Elizabethan playhouses were typically circular or polygonal wooden structures with a central open-air yard. The stage projected into this yard, and three tiers of covered galleries surrounded it. ‘Groundlings’ — ordinary people who paid a penny — stood in the open yard around the stage, while wealthier patrons sat in the covered galleries. The stage was large and thrust into the audience, allowing for different acting areas and creating intimacy. There was no scenery in the modern sense; location was established through words and the audience’s imagination. Performances took place in the afternoon by natural light. Audiences were mixed and lively — eating, drinking, talking and reacting noisily.

Key Fact

The first permanent public playhouse in England was “The Theatre,” built in Shoreditch, London, in 1576 by James Burbage. The Globe Theatre, built in Southwark in 1599, became the most famous Elizabethan playhouse and was closely associated with William Shakespeare.

Attitudes Towards the Theatre

Not everyone welcomed the new playhouses. The Puritans strongly opposed the theatre on moral and religious grounds. They argued that plays encouraged immorality, that theatres were dens of crime and disease, and that performances on Sundays competed with church attendance. London’s city authorities largely agreed, which is why the early playhouses were built just outside the city boundaries — in the “Liberties,” areas beyond the jurisdiction of the city council.

In 1597 the city authorities briefly ordered the demolition of all London’s playhouses, though this was never fully carried out. The theatre had powerful patrons, however: noble families sponsored acting companies (the Chamberlain’s Men were under the patronage of the Lord Chamberlain, and later became the King’s Men under James I). Elizabeth herself enjoyed theatrical performances; she had plays performed at court regularly. This royal favour helped protect the theatre industry from its opponents.

William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was the most celebrated playwright of the Elizabethan age, though he was one of many talented writers working in this period. Christopher Marlowe, Ben Jonson and Thomas Kyd were among his contemporaries. Plays ranged from histories (presenting English kings and their struggles) to tragedies, comedies and romances. The popular appeal of theatre was broad: a wealthy patron and a penny-paying groundling might watch the same play. This cultural breadth made the theatre unusual — few other forms of entertainment crossed so many social boundaries.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Describe two features’ questions on Elizabethan entertainment, be specific: don’t just write “the theatre was popular” — name the Globe, give 1599 as its date, or mention that groundlings paid a penny. For 8-mark significance questions on the theatre, address both its immediate cultural significance (a new commercial entertainment industry) and its long-term legacy (the foundation of a continuous theatrical tradition in England). For 6-mark cause questions about Puritan opposition, chain your reasons: Puritans believed theatres encouraged idleness and immorality, drew people away from church and allowed diseases to spread in large crowds — each point needs development to access higher marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Elizabethan entertainment ranged from cruel sports (bear-baiting, cock-fighting) enjoyed by all classes, to court masques, hunting and hawking for the wealthy. These were normal, accepted pastimes, opposed by Puritans for moral rather than animal-welfare reasons.
  • The professional theatre was the most significant cultural development of the age: the first permanent playhouse was built in 1576, and the Globe Theatre opened in 1599, closely linked to William Shakespeare and the Lord Chamberlain’s Men.
  • Puritans and London city authorities opposed the theatre as immoral and disruptive to church attendance, but royal patronage — Elizabeth attended court performances regularly — helped protect the industry from suppression.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of bear-baiting as a form of Elizabethan entertainment.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with supporting detail, e.g. bear-baiting took place in purpose-built bear gardens on London's south bank, where a chained bear was attacked by dogs (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature without specific detail (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the design of an Elizabethan playhouse.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: precise feature with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: circular or polygonal wooden structure with an open central yard; covered galleries on three levels for wealthier patrons; a thrust stage projecting into the yard; groundlings stood in the yard for a penny; performances in daylight with no artificial scenery. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Puritan opposition to the Elizabethan theatre.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a detailed causal chain with evidence, e.g. Puritans believed theatre performances on Sundays competed directly with church attendance — audiences who went to see a play on a Sunday afternoon were not attending worship, undermining religious observance and giving the devil a foothold in everyday life. Secure: a clear cause with some supporting evidence. Developing: a relevant cause with limited development. Emerging: a simple statement. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the building of the first permanent playhouses in the 1570s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (created a commercial theatre industry; enabled regular professional performances; attracted playwrights like Marlowe and Shakespeare) AND over time (established a tradition of English theatre; Southwark as a cultural hub; the Globe). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation with limited range. Emerging: simple descriptive points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a Puritan pamphlet attacking theatres as 'dens of vice' for understanding attitudes towards the theatre in Elizabethan England?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (what the pamphlet argues), provenance (a Puritan author — one-sided, religious perspective) and contextual knowledge (Puritan opposition real and consistent; but theatres also had royal patronage and noble sponsors) to give a substantiated judgement about utility and limitations. Secure: addresses two of three elements. Developing: mainly describes the source. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'The Elizabethan theatre was the most important form of popular entertainment in Elizabethan England.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: argues for (professional playhouses drew large cross-class audiences; associated with Shakespeare; protected by royal and noble patronage; new cultural form) AND against (cruel sports drew larger daily audiences; court entertainment was more socially significant for the elite; theatre was concentrated in London) before a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: both sides with evidence and a conclusion. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: simple agreement. Maximum 12 marks.

knowledge_checks.q: In what year was the first permanent public playhouse — 'The Theatre' — built in London?
Why were the early Elizabethan playhouses built just outside the city of London?
options: Land was cheaper outside the city
The Queen preferred performances away from the city centre
The playhouses needed open countryside for large audiences
They were located in the Liberties, beyond the city council's jurisdiction

knowledge_checks.q: The Globe Theatre was built in Southwark in _____ by the company known as the Lord Chamberlain's Men.
People who paid a penny to stand in the open yard of an Elizabethan playhouse were known as _____.
Match each Elizabethan entertainment to its key feature:
right: A chained bear attacked by dogs in a purpose-built arena
An elaborate court entertainment of music, dance and costumes
The most famous Elizabethan playhouse, built in Southwark in 1599

flashcard_questions.a: A popular entertainment where a chained bear was attacked by dogs in a purpose-built bear garden.

flashcard_questions.q: Who enjoyed bear-baiting in Elizabethan England?
flashcard_questions.a: All social classes, including Elizabeth I herself.

flashcard_questions.q: When and where was the first permanent English playhouse built?
flashcard_questions.a: 1576, in Shoreditch, London, by James Burbage.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Globe Theatre and when was it built?
flashcard_questions.a: A playhouse in Southwark, built in 1599 by the Lord Chamberlain's Men, closely linked to Shakespeare.

flashcard_questions.q: What were 'groundlings' in the Elizabethan theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: Audience members who paid a penny to stand in the open yard around the stage.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Puritans oppose the theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: They believed it encouraged immorality, gambling and idleness, and drew people away from church.

flashcard_questions.q: Why were early playhouses built in the Liberties outside the city of London?
flashcard_questions.a: To avoid the jurisdiction of the city council, which opposed them.
An elaborate entertainment combining music, dance, poetry and magnificent costumes, performed for the monarch.

flashcard_questions.q: What protected the Elizabethan theatre from being shut down by its opponents?
flashcard_questions.a: Royal and noble patronage — Elizabeth herself enjoyed theatrical performances at court.

flashcard_questions.q: Who were the Lord Chamberlain's Men?
flashcard_questions.a: The acting company that built the Globe Theatre; later renamed the King's Men under James I.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one Elizabethan playwright other than Shakespeare.
flashcard_questions.a: Christopher Marlowe (or Ben Jonson or Thomas Kyd).

flashcard_questions.q: What made the Elizabethan playhouse design unusual compared to earlier performances?
flashcard_questions.a: It was a permanent circular structure with a thrust stage, covered galleries and an open yard.

glossary_terms.definition: A popular Elizabethan entertainment in which a chained bear was attacked by dogs, taking place in purpose-built bear gardens.
An Elizabethan blood sport in which two roosters were set to fight each other in a cockpit, drawing large crowds and gambling.
An elaborate theatrical entertainment combining music, dancing, speech and spectacular costumes, performed at court for the monarch and nobility.
A purpose-built permanent theatre, the first of which opened in Elizabethan London, transforming theatre into a regular commercial entertainment.
The playhouse built in Southwark in 1599 by the Lord Chamberlain's Men, closely associated with William Shakespeare.
Strict Protestant reformers who opposed what they saw as immoral or irreligious entertainments, including theatre and cruel sports.
